metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Because the experimental design pits TTB against Tallying on almost all trials (where the highest validity cue favors one option and the sheer number of cues favors the other), TTB simulated agents will have a high score on this metric, whereas Tallying agents will have a low score.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing the option favored by the highest-validity cue (cue 0) between trials where the overall tally strongly supports that same option (tally difference >= 3) and trials where the overall tally opposes or ties it (tally difference <= 0). For Take The Best, cue 0 is the only cue ever consulted, so the choice probability is insensitive to the remaining cues, yielding a metric near 0. For Tallying, choice probability is driven entirely by the tally difference, meaning the subject will frequently choose the cue 0 winner when the tally strongly agrees, but will guess or choose the other option when the tally disagrees, yielding a large positive metric.

Take The Best (TTB) is a non-compensatory heuristic that relies solely on the highest-validity discriminating cue, ignoring all other features. Consequently, TTB predicts identical choice probabilities across all trial pairs, meaning a subject's adherence to TTB should be uniformly high across all pairs (subject only to constant lapse and softmax noise). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all cues, so its confidence fluctuates depending on the degree of cue conflict. On trials where lower-validity cues strongly oppose the best cue, WADD's adherence to the TTB prediction drops significantly. By calculating the minimum TTB adherence across all 8 unique trial pairs for each subject, we capture this localized drop. TTB will maintain a high minimum adherence, whereas WADD will exhibit a much lower minimum due to its compensatory weighting on conflicting trials.

In this experimental design, the first discriminating cue favors Option A in every single trial. Therefore, Take The Best (TTB) consistently predicts Option A across the entire experiment, resulting in a high overall probability of choosing A (averaging ~85%, constrained only by the lapse rate). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model predicts a significantly lower overall proportion of A choices. For high values of gamma (>4), the centered validities shrink to near-zero, causing WADD to predict ~50/50 guessing. For low values of gamma (<2), WADD behaves compensatorily and favors Option B in trials where B has a strong advantage in lower-validity cues (e.g., Trials 1, 2, and 6). Thus, simply measuring the overall proportion of Option A choices provides a robust, large-effect-size discriminator between the two models.

To robustly separate Random Guessing from the WADD model across all its parameter regimes (especially extreme values of gamma), we focus exclusively on the trials where the evidence is overwhelmingly asymmetric. In Trials 7 and 8, Option B possesses the top 3 most valid features while Option A lacks them, making B strictly preferred by WADD regardless of whether the subject uses equal weighting (gamma=0) or heavily overweighs the first feature (high gamma). In Trials 1 and 2, Option A possesses the top 3 features. Under Random Guessing, the difference in the rate of choosing B between these two trial sets is exactly 0. Under WADD, this difference will always be strictly positive because the model's preference direction is invariant to gamma on these specific trials, thereby reducing between-subject variance and maximizing the mean gap.

This metric calculates the accuracy on 'dominance' trials, where one option has all positive expert ratings and the other has none. The Weighted Additive (WADD) model, regardless of its specific parameters (except for extremely high lapse rates), will overwhelmingly choose the dominant option. In contrast, the Random Guessing model predicts exactly 50% accuracy on these same trials. By isolating the trials with the strongest signal-to-noise ratio, this metric maximizes the mean difference between the two theories while minimizing the within-theory variance.
